node.label: Samuel P. Huntington
node.date_label: 1957: The Soldier and the State: The Theory and Politics of Civil-Military Relations · 1968: Political Order in Changing Societies · 1993: The Clash of Civilizations? (Foreign Affairs article) · 1996: The Clash of Civilizations and the Remaking of World Order
node.description: A political scientist whose development arguments distinguish political institutionalization from economic growth and electoral form. His later civilizational model remains a subject of controversy; Edward Said criticized its treatment of internally diverse societies as coherent opposing civilizations.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Soldier and the State: The Theory and Politics of Civil-Military Relations (1957); Political Order in Changing Societies (1968); The Clash of Civilizations? (Foreign Affairs article) (1993); The Clash of Civilizations and the Remaking of World Order (1996).

proposed_edges.relationship: Distinguishes political capacity and institutionalization from regime form and economic modernization.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own Political Order opening p. 1 and preserved prior source review support the distinction. This does not endorse order-first political prescriptions or verify national comparisons and predictions.

proposed_edges.relationship: Criticizes the civilizational model for personifying Islam and the West and suppressing their internal diversity and exchanges.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Said’s own 2001 essay opening read. Edge is Said’s specific criticism of Huntington, with explicit attribution; Huntington’s whole 1996 book and complete reception debate unread.

new_sources.title: Edward Said, The Clash of Ignorance, The Nation (4 October 2001; print issue 22 October 2001)

verification.note: Opening through discussion of personified Islam and West read: identifies Huntington’s summer 1993 Foreign Affairs article and criticizes suppression of internal diversity, exchanges and complexities. Rest of essay unread here. Online and print dates distinguished. Criticism attributed to Said, not treated as an impartial verdict or evidence that all readers agreed.
